analysis.one_liner: Halts new offshore oil and gas leasing and drilling off California's coast for roughly a decade.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Resources Committee's subcommittee and died without a vote at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have told the Interior Department not to sell or issue any new oil and gas leases in the waters off Southern, Central, and Northern California, and not to approve any exploration plans or drilling permits there, until early 2005 or until Congress received completed environmental studies reviewed by independent scientists. In practice it would have put new offshore drilling off California on hold for years while the science was filled in. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, sent to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: California coastal communities and residents who face the risk of oil spills and drilling-related industrialization of the coastline, plus the tourism and commercial fishing businesses whose livelihoods depend on an undrilled coast. Future generations of Californians keep a coastline without new offshore platforms while the environmental questions are studied.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California coastal communities, tourism, and fishing

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred the Interior Secretary from holding lease sales or issuing oil and gas leases in the Southern, Central, and Northern California planning areas until January 1, 2005, or until Congress received a final environmental statement for the next five-year leasing program plus 45 days of continuous congressional session [S3].

It also blocked approval of any exploration plan, development plan, or drilling permit off California until required environmental studies—based on gaps identified by a 1989 National Research Council report—were completed and peer-reviewed by at least three independent scientists nominated by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and approved by the Interior Secretary and California's Governor [S3].

The CRS summary confirms the moratorium covered preleasing, leasing, exploration, and development activities in all three California planning areas, with studies submitted to Congress during the moratorium period [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that wanted to lease, explore, or drill in federal waters off California, which would have been locked out for years. The federal government and taxpayers would also forgo any bonus bids and royalties those leases might have produced, and energy consumers bear a marginal cost from reduced potential domestic supply.

drawbacks.text: Blocking new leasing and drilling off California would reduce potential domestic oil and gas production, forgoing federal royalty revenue and a marginal addition to energy supply [S3].

The bill's unusual trigger—45 days of 'continuous session' of Congress after the studies were submitted, with days when either chamber adjourned more than three days excluded—could have stretched the moratorium indefinitely if the studies were never finished [S3].

A good-faith critic could argue that Congress was substituting a statutory freeze for the ordinary environmental review and leasing process under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, rather than letting that process run [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Californians the tradeoff was straightforward: a decade of certainty against new offshore drilling, in exchange for lost federal revenue and a marginal loss of potential energy supply. The main design weakness is that the moratorium's endpoint depended on studies being completed and Congress staying continuously in session, which could have turned a 'temporary' moratorium into a de facto permanent ban. Opponents of offshore drilling would consider that a feature; supporters of expanded drilling would consider it a flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 104th Congress, referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1997 without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy (Duke) Cunningham introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, with nine cosponsors—six Republicans and three Democrats [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee the same day [S5].

On January 17, 1995, it was referred to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and Interior was asked for an executive comment—routine early steps—and it advanced no further in the two-year Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in subcommittee with no vote ever taken in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests were better off because the bill died: nothing stood in the way of the ordinary Interior Department leasing process off California, and no statutory moratorium was ever enacted from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Randy 'Duke' Cunningham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the moratorium bill on the first day of the 104th Congress.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (6 of 234 House Republicans, 3 of 198 House Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small but bipartisan support.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referring it to the subcommittee on January 17, 1995; it received no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan but tiny: of its 10 sponsors, 7 were Republicans (including the sponsor) and 3 were Democrats, and opposition never took the form of a recorded vote—the bill simply never advanced [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred new leases, exploration plans, and drilling permits in all three California offshore planning areas until roughly 2005 [S3]. The industry's interest in continuing to lease and drill off the California coast runs against coastal residents' interest in avoiding spills and new platforms.

industries.industry: California coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: An undrilled coast preserves the beaches, ocean views, and fisheries these industries depend on; their interest in blocking new offshore platforms runs alongside that of coastal residents.
